why: Level was decided earlier. 'I am want' (be + base verb) is a real learner mistake, and 'I'm wanting' is the card's state-verb point (present_simple watch: 'State verbs (know, like, want, need, believe) stay simple'); informal 'I'm wanting' is not the taught norm.

'Both sound the same' and 'Both sound permanent' are believable misunderstandings of the difference the card teaches ('A permanent situation: present simple; a temporary one: continuous: I live in Riga. I'm living with my parents this year.'), not illogical fillers.
'Yesterday' is the time word the rules ask for (29 October: an unambiguous time word, not an open context); the wrong options are wrong with it. Level was decided earlier.
Reader 2 only confirms the task: contracted and full forms of both the past simple and the past perfect are already accepted.
Only level flags; past continuous + when is on the B1.1 card ('A longer action interrupted by a short action'), and 'were walking' with I is the card's mistake type ('They [[was]] waiting').
'already five years' is a real mistake of Latvian learners (jau piecus gadus); 'already' is on the present_perfect card ('already before the main verb'). Level was decided earlier.
The time word deciding the tense is the point (card: 'I [[have seen]] him yesterday' → 'I saw him yesterday'). 'have saw' is the card's mistake type ('She has [[went]] home'), so it stays.
'yesterday' is the time word that makes the past simple necessary, as the card's mistake 'I have seen him yesterday' shows; this is the point of the task, not a giveaway.
'have been work' is the card's own mistake ('She has been [[work]] all day'); 'have working' is a believable missing-been form and 'had been working' is wrong with 'I'm still at my desk'.
Fixed in r21 (dropped 'She has run'). 'She is running' is the believable mistake the explanation answers; ease alone is no reason to change it.

Both readers: 'were playing', 'played' and 'have played' are also correct English for a just-finished activity, and no gap context can rule out the past. Turned into a choice with card-only wrong options ('I [[am waiting]] for an hour' type: are playing, contradicted by 'washing their hands now'; 'She has been [[work]]' type: have been play), so only the form decides. fix.q: Choose the correct option: The children are washing their hands now. Look at the floor! They ___ with paint.
fix.why: They have stopped (they are washing their hands now), but the floor shows what they were doing: *They have been playing with paint.* *Are playing* would mean they are still playing.
fix.why_lv: Viņi ir beiguši (tagad viņi mazgā rokas), bet grīda rāda, ko viņi darīja: *They have been playing with paint.* *Are playing* nozīmētu, ka viņi joprojām spēlējas.

All three wrong options are the card's mistake types: 'I [[will to]] help you', a missing be ('She [[going to]] call you' → 'about to') and a missing to ('is about'); the card teaches '*be about to* = very soon'.

Readers: 'It's about to rain' is correct and is a card form ('*be about to*: the very near future'), but the first check wanted only going to; the second check takes 'Shall I' while its message named only I'll / I will. Both checks and messages aligned. 'It might rain' is rejected (not on the future card, and it says a possibility, not what you expect); 'It will rain' is rejected by the card and Murphy: with evidence now, going to ('Look at the clouds! It's going to rain').

Ko rāda mākoņi, saki ar *going to* (vai *about to*) + pamatforma.
\b(i'll|i’ll|i will|shall i)\b

fix.q: Choose the correct option: We won't finish on time ___ someone helps us.
fix.why: *Unless* = *if ... not*: *We won't finish on time unless someone helps us* (= if nobody helps us).
fix.why_lv: *Unless* = *if ... not*: *We won't finish on time unless someone helps us* (= ja neviens mums nepalīdzēs).

fix.q: You want to join an evening Italian course at a language school, but the website shows no start date. Write one polite question to the school.
must: \b(could|can|would) you (please )?(tell me|let me know|check|find out|confirm)\b|\bwould you mind (telling me|checking)\b|\bdo you (happen to )?know\b|\bi[\'’]?d like to know\b|\bi would like to know\b|\bi (was )?wonder(ing)?\b
Start politely: *Could you tell me …?*, *Do you know …?* or *I'd like to know …*
Sāc pieklājīgi: *Could you tell me …?*, *Do you know …?* vai *I'd like to know …*
\b(tell me|let me know|check|find out|confirm|telling me|checking|know|wonder|wondering),?\s+(please,?\s+)?((on|at|in|from) )?(if|whether|when|what|where|why|how|who|which)\b
Then a question word or *if*: *… when the next course starts*.
Tad jautājamais vārds vai *if*: *… when the next course starts*.

^(?!.*\b(if|whether|when|where|why|who|how(?:\s+(?:long|soon|much|many|often|far)(?:\s+\w+)?)?|what(?:\s+\w+)?|which(?:\s+\w+)?)\s+(?:(?:do|does|did|is|are|was|were|has|have|had|could|would|should)(?:n[\'’]t)?|will|won[\'’]t|can|can[\'’]t|cannot)\s+(you|he|she|it|they|we|i|the|my|your|our|his|her|their|this|that|these|those|someone|somebody|anyone|anybody|there|mine)\b)
After the question word the subject comes first, with no *do / does*: *when the course starts*, not *when does the course start*.
Pēc jautājamā vārda sākumā ir teikuma priekšmets, bez *do / does*: *when the course starts*, nevis *when does the course start*.
^(?!.*\b(?:when|where|why|what time|what day|what date|how much|how long|how soon|how often)\s+(?!(?:is|was|has|does)\b)\w+s\s+(?:the|my|your|our|his|her|their|this|that)\b)
Put the subject before the verb: *when the course starts*, not *when starts the course*.
Teikuma priekšmets ir pirms darbības vārda: *when the course starts*, nevis *when starts the course*.
fix.why: A polite start, then *when* and the order of a statement, with no *does*: *Could you tell me when the next Italian course starts?*
fix.why_lv: Pieklājīgs sākums, tad *when* un vārdu secība kā apgalvojumā, bez *does*: *Could you tell me when the next Italian course starts?*

fix.q: You ordered a printer online ten days ago, and you are still waiting. Write one polite question to the shop's customer service.
must: \b(could|can|would) you (please )?(tell me|let me know|check|find out|confirm)\b|\bwould you mind (telling me|checking)\b|\bdo you (happen to )?know\b|\bi[\'’]?d like to know\b|\bi would like to know\b|\bi (was )?wonder(ing)?\b
Start politely: *Could you tell me …?*, *Do you know …?* or *I'd like to know …*
Sāc pieklājīgi: *Could you tell me …?*, *Do you know …?* vai *I'd like to know …*
\b(tell me|let me know|check|find out|confirm|telling me|checking|know|wonder|wondering),?\s+(please,?\s+)?((on|at|in|from) )?(if|whether|when|what|where|why|how|who|which)\b
Then *if* (or *whether*) or a question word: *… if you have sent my order*, *… when my printer will arrive*.
Tad *if* (vai *whether*) vai jautājamais vārds: *… if you have sent my order*, *… when my printer will arrive*.

^(?!.*\b(if|whether|when|where|why|who|how(?:\s+(?:long|soon|much|many|often|far)(?:\s+\w+)?)?|what(?:\s+\w+)?|which(?:\s+\w+)?)\s+(?:(?:do|does|did|is|are|was|were|has|have|had|could|would|should)(?:n[\'’]t)?|will|won[\'’]t|can|can[\'’]t|cannot)\s+(you|he|she|it|they|we|i|the|my|your|our|his|her|their|this|that|these|those|someone|somebody|anyone|anybody|there|mine)\b)
After *if* or the question word the subject comes first, with no *did*: *if you sent my order*, *when my printer will arrive*.
Pēc *if* vai jautājamā vārda sākumā ir teikuma priekšmets, bez *did*: *if you sent my order*, *when my printer will arrive*.
^(?!.*\b(?:when|where|why|what time|what day|what date|how much|how long|how soon|how often)\s+(?!(?:is|was|has|does)\b)\w+s\s+(?:the|my|your|our|his|her|their|this|that)\b)
Put the subject before the verb: *when my printer arrives*, not *when arrives my printer*.
Teikuma priekšmets ir pirms darbības vārda: *when my printer arrives*, nevis *when arrives my printer*.
fix.why: A polite start, then *if* and the order of a statement: *Could you tell me if you have sent my order yet?* With *did* in the direct question, the verb itself is in the past: *if you sent my order*.
fix.why_lv: Pieklājīgs sākums, tad *if* un vārdu secība kā apgalvojumā: *Could you tell me if you have sent my order yet?* Ja tiešajā jautājumā ir *did*, pagātni rāda darbības vārds: *if you sent my order*.

fix.correct: If metal gets hot, it expand.
wrong: When I travel by bus, I always feel sick.
If you don't save your work, you lose it.
Whenever my neighbour plays music, my dog barks.
fix.why: In a general truth both parts use the present simple, and after *it* the verb takes *-s*: *If metal gets hot, it expands.*
fix.why_lv: Vispārīgā patiesībā abās daļās lieto Present Simple, un pēc *it* darbības vārdam ir galotne *-s*: *If metal gets hot, it expands.*

why: 'They won't let you in if you show your ticket' makes no sense here, so 'if' does not fit; 'unless' is the card's 'if … not'. All options are card words ('if, unless, as soon as, when').
Reader 2: 'If I went, I would meet her' does not say 'I'm not going'; it is an unlikely future. The card is changed to what the sentence means, still not swappable with the other two.

pairs: If I had gone, I would have met her.
If I hadn't gone, I wouldn't have met her.
If I went, I would meet her.
fix.why: *If I had gone*: I didn't go. *If I hadn't gone*: I went. *If I went, I would meet her*: an unlikely future, so I probably won't go.
fix.why_lv: *If I had gone*: es negāju. *If I hadn't gone*: es gāju. *If I went, I would meet her*: maz ticama nākotne, tātad es visticamāk neiešu.
